newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australian Commodities Roundup - Oct 21.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australian Commodities Roundup - Oct 21.

text.p: Lead prices tumbled towards their lowest levels of the year on Friday in a sell-off that reflected big deliveries from China.

Traders said there were also signs that demand was weak. Western motorists were not rushing to renew lead-acid car batteries unless they had to, because they were deterred by high garage forecourt prices.

But oil prices soared to the highest levels since the 1991 Gulf War on Friday as cold weather swept into the northern United States and both traders and government officials worried about low heating oil stocks.
In Chicago, the CRB Commodity Index fell 0.77 points to 243.35.

Crude oil futures on the NYMEX ended at a new post-Gulf War high on Friday as cold weather moved in on the northeast U.S., leaving the market in a bullish technical position, traders said. November crude oil futures on the NYMEX closed at $25.78, their highest since January, 1991 in the midst of the Gulf War. Friday's intra-day high was $25.85, beating the $25.70 post-Gulf War high set last April and matched earlier this week. Friday's

move was a continuation of the bull trend since the end of July, which has been led by heating oil and pushed crude futures up by almost 30 pct, traders said. "Continued Iraqi tensions, colder weather, lack of government action" combined on Friday to help push the market higher, said Thomas Blakeslee, a trader and analyst at Cargill Investors Service. November heat oil settled at 74.06 cents a gallon, up 177 points on the day, and gasoline November futures settled up 141 points at 67.94 cents a gallon, with the intra-day high of 68.15 not far off the contract high of 68.75 cents.

Lead prices took a hammering in Friday LME trading, with a depressed market dropping to its lowest levels since end-January and looking like falling further, traders said. Other metals finished mixed with copper closing on a positive note after a large LME warehouse inventory fall, although the market baulked at $1,950 again. Lead was pummelled lower during the afternoon rings and kerb, with the breach of $730 triggering speculative sell-stops down to a low of $715 before a last trade at $719, down $13. Despite being oversold, a test of $700 is likely, they said. Traders said the upcoming battery season and expected

better demand from the auto sector is as yet having little impact on a market grappling with negative sentiment. Also, stocks are rising and the Chinese are exporting more metal at present, analysts noted. Copper prices fluctuated, unable to penetrate $1,950, but supported on dips which kept the market in the plus column. Underlying sentiment was helped by a large 19,125-tonne stock fall, although there are doubts over how much is actual offtake. Copper is moving out of a wide range of geographical locations, and although some is going into consumption significant tonnages reflect arbitrage with New York and China. Final kerb business was at $1,940, up $16 a tonne.

Cash/threes finished at a slightly wider $32/34 backwardation, reflecting metal lent to the market in the summer now departing. Total LME inventory of 172,425 tonnes is the lowest for a year. Aluminium's recent mini-rally faltered at expected tough resistance around $1,375, and with stocks rising 4,300 tonnes the market retreated to end the session at $1,359, down $10. Zinc hardly moved throughout the day, ending at $1,019, up just $1 a tonne. The nickel market was unexciting throughout the session, with business restricted to a tight, generally lower, range. Prices were on the defensive under $7,100 after a 546-tonne stock increase, and last trade was at $7,055, a $25

loss. Tin edged away from its floor, but there were few features in a slow market, and last trade was at $5,975, up just $20. COMEX copper ended slightly firmer after trading within a narrow range as a bullish large drop in LME stocks was countered by the bearish return to work at the Kennecott smelter in Utah.

CBOT wheat futures closed lower and new contract lows were set as the market remains plagued by steep U.S. wheat prices relative to other wheat-producing countries, traders said. "Wheat can't rally at these levels, we could break a dime and

still be overpriced compared with other countries," a trader said. The new contract low for March was $3.94 per bushel, below the previous low of $3.99-1/2 set Thursday. Wheat dropped despite a bigger-than-expected number in USDA's weekly export sales report. USDA early Friday said U.S. wheat exports during the week ended October 10 totaled 737,000 tonnes, more than double the previous week and 75 percent above the four-week average. Technicians said before the open Friday, the four- and 20-day moving averages were giving off bearish signals. First resistance for December was at $4.16 per bushel and second resistance was at $4.24-1/2. The session high for December was

$4.13. First support was at $4.07-1/2 and second support at $3.99. Wheat closed three to 6-1/4 cents per bushel lower, with December down 6-1/4 at $4.04-3/4. Fund selling led the way down with Smith Barney a key seller of two million bushels of December and Dean Witter Reynolds also sold two million December, traders said. Wheat futures volume was estimated at 17,000 contracts, down from 21,751 Thursday, according to the CBOT. In wheat options, Smith Barney bought 1,500 March $4.80 calls at 1-1/2 cents and FIMAT Futures bought 1,50 March $4.80 calls at 1-1/2 cents, traders said. Wheat options volume was estimated by the CBOT at 15,000 contracts, up from 6,190

New York precious metals futures ended mostly lower Friday, with gold and silver down for the third day in a row, leaving the complex finishing the week on a bearish note, analysts said. There wasn't much activity today, but the the market ended the week looking soft, despite some shortcovering of locals near the close," North American Equity Services floor trader John Geraghty said. COMEX December gold ended down 50 cents at $382.10 an ounce, slipping to a two week intraday low at

$381.60. However, COMEX gold stocks fell 965 ounces to 1,053,329 ounces Thursday, and are at their lowest levels since November 1977. In New York bullion trade, gold ended quoted $380.10/380.50, against the London Friday afternoon fix at $380.00, and the New York close Thursday at $380.35/380.85. But the key $380 support level, which has held since April 1995, remained intact again Friday, traders noted. COMEX December silver ended down 0.5 cent at $4.897 an ounce, though Thursday's intraday low at $4.880 was not breached. COMEX silver stocks were unchanged Thursday at 130,794,680, after seeing a ten year low earlier this week, but traders said inventories in other
countries were ample. The spot gold/silver ratio ended at 77.7, little changed from Thursday's close, after a the ratio fell to 75.4 in the past week, when silver was recovering.

CSCE world sugar futures closed an active session weaker, but trade buying managed to carry the spot-March contract out from under major support, where it traded in early dealings, market sources said. Light fund selling began when the March contract reached the day's high of 10.84. The buying dried up and the selling accelerated around the previous low of 10.69.

Nearby support remains at 10.60 but longer term support was pegged at 10.55. Resistance was seen at 10.80. One broker suggested players had been long in anticipation of Hurricane Lili. But it is too soon to gauge damage to Cuba's sugar crop, which accounts for less than five percent of world output. "No one is very concerned about it," the broker said." The spot-March contract settled down 0.13 to 10.64, ranged 10.84 to 10.55. The back months closed 0.11 to 0.02 lower. Volume was estimated to have reached a brisk 21,983 lots. Most market sources see prices heading even lower as demand is not likely to keep pace with supply. International Sugar Organization (ISO)
today put world sugar production at 123.8 million tonnes raw value in 1996/97, market sources said. ISO said a surplus of 2.5 million tonnes could push prices towards 10.00 cents per lb.
